title: Chapter 3 Drill: Wound Healing, Infection, Immunology, and Hematology

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a drained perforated appendix with a well-controlled source and recovers with normal temperature, white count, and bowel function. How long should antibiotics be continued after adequate source control?
options: Fourteen days regardless of clinical progress
Until the drain output has fully stopped and the drain is removed
About four days, then stop once clinical resolution is evident
Six weeks to prevent late abscess formation
items.explanation: Trials of complicated intra-abdominal infection show that a short fixed course of about four days after adequate source control gives outcomes equal to longer courses. Extending therapy to two weeks or more adds adverse effects and resistance. Drain output does not determine the endpoint. Six weeks is for bone or endovascular infection. Persistent signs after four days should prompt a search for undrained disease, not simply more drugs, because source control is what determines success.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman on long-term oral prednisone for rheumatoid arthritis has delayed healing after a skin graft donor site. Which vitamin supplement is most likely to partially reverse the steroid effect on wound healing?
options: Vitamin A, which counters steroid-related inflammatory suppression
Vitamin K, which restores clotting factor synthesis in liver disease
Vitamin E, which strengthens collagen cross-links
Vitamin B12, which supports erythrocyte maturation
items.explanation: Glucocorticoids impair macrophage function, fibroblast activity, and collagen synthesis, and topical or oral vitamin A can partly restore the inflammatory response. Vitamin K affects clotting, not repair. Vitamin E has no proven benefit and large doses may impair healing. Vitamin B12 corrects megaloblastic anemia but does not offset steroid effects. Vitamin C remains essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with diabetes has a painful, rapidly spreading thigh erythema with bullae and crepitus. He is febrile and hypotensive. Pain is out of proportion to the findings. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Computed tomography before any intervention
Emergency operative debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics
Oral antibiotics and close outpatient follow-up
Aspiration of the bullae with warm compresses
items.explanation: Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, and shock indicate necrotizing soft tissue infection, a surgical emergency in which mortality rises with every hour of delay. Treatment is prompt wide debridement with broad coverage including anaerobes and clindamycin for toxin suppression. Imaging should never delay surgery in a patient who is unstable. Oral therapy and compresses cannot control the process. Repeat debridement is often needed.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an international normalized ratio of 9 and a subdural hematoma on head imaging. What is the most appropriate reversal regimen?
options: Oral vitamin K alone with a repeat level tomorrow
Fresh frozen plasma alone at a low dose given over several hours
Withholding warfarin only and observing
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate with intravenous vitamin K
items.explanation: Life-threatening bleeding on warfarin requires immediate replacement of the vitamin K dependent factors with prothrombin complex concentrate, which corrects the ratio within minutes, plus intravenous vitamin K for sustained effect because factor half-lives are short. Oral vitamin K acts too slowly. Plasma needs large volumes and is slower. Observation alone permits expansion of the hemorrhage.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman on a ventilator for five days develops a new fever, purulent tracheal secretions, and a new infiltrate. Which empiric strategy best fits ventilator-associated pneumonia in this setting?
options: Give a single oral agent chosen for convenience and low cost to start
Cover resistant gram-negative bacteria and staphylococci, then narrow to culture results
Withhold treatment until all cultures are final, which takes several days
Use narrow penicillin therapy for every patient
items.explanation: Late-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia carries a high risk of resistant organisms including pseudomonas and methicillin-resistant staphylococci, so empiric therapy should be broad, guided by local antibiograms, and then narrowed at 48 to 72 hours using culture data. Oral convenience therapy is unreliable in critical illness. Waiting for final cultures risks death. Narrow penicillin therapy misses the likely pathogens.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man with massive hemorrhage from a pelvic fracture receives a massive transfusion protocol. Which ratio of red cells, plasma, and platelets is recommended?
options: Red cells alone, given until hemoglobin has normalized completely
Plasma only, with no red cells for the first hour
Four red cell units for each unit of platelets
A balanced ratio near one to one to one
items.explanation: Damage control resuscitation uses balanced transfusion near a one to one to one ratio of red cells, plasma, and platelets, which approximates whole blood and limits dilutional coagulopathy. Red cells alone worsen coagulopathy and acidosis. Plasma alone does not restore oxygen delivery. A ratio dominated by red cells reproduces dilution. Early tranexamic acid and calcium support the protocol.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man in the intensive care unit has a central venous catheter placed nine days ago. He now has fever and positive blood cultures with Staphylococcus aureus, and the insertion site is clean. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Remove the catheter, give targeted intravenous therapy, and obtain echocardiography
Treat through the line with a short oral course of antibiotics and no removal of the line
Exchange the catheter over a guidewire and continue
Culture the tip and stop any further workup
items.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia from a catheter requires removal of the device, effective intravenous therapy, repeat cultures to document clearance, and echocardiography to look for endocarditis, with a longer course if complications exist. Oral therapy and treating through the line risk relapse. Guidewire exchange leaves colonized tubing in the vessel. Tip culture alone provides no treatment plan.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy with recurrent sinus infections, absent tonsils, and very low serum immunoglobulins of all classes needs an inguinal hernia repair. Which statement about this patient is correct?
options: He is at risk mainly for fungal infection due to neutrophil failure
He needs live vaccines before the operation
Lack of B cells predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infection, and replacement immunoglobulin may be given
His wound healing will be unaffected by his condition
items.explanation: Absent tonsils and panhypogammaglobulinemia suggest X-linked agammaglobulinemia, a B cell defect that leaves patients vulnerable to encapsulated bacteria and enteroviruses. Immunoglobulin replacement lowers infection rates and the surgical plan should include prophylaxis and careful hygiene. Fungal risk marks neutrophil disorders. Live vaccines are contraindicated. Infection can impair healing, so perioperative care is planned with the immunology team.

items.stem: An intensive care patient has a wound culture growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus with a vancomycin minimum inhibitory concentration of 1. Which infection-control measure is the most effective at stopping spread between patients?
options: Routine prophylactic vancomycin for every patient in neighboring beds
Closing the unit to all new admissions for a full year, with no exceptions
Wearing a surgical mask during all patient contact
Hand hygiene with contact precautions and dedicated equipment
items.explanation: Resistant organisms spread mainly on hands and shared equipment, so hand hygiene, gown and glove contact precautions, and dedicated devices are the proven measures, with screening and decolonization in selected units. Mass prophylaxis breeds more resistance. Unit closure is disproportionate and unsupported. Masks guard against droplets but do little against contact transmission. Antibiotic stewardship also lowers selection pressure.

items.stem: A patient on aspirin and clopidogrel for a recent coronary stent needs an elective hernia repair. Which approach is the best?
options: Stop both agents at once and operate this week while platelets recover and bleeding risk falls
Give platelet transfusion before the skin incision
Defer elective surgery until the minimum stent therapy period has passed
Continue both agents and reverse them with vitamin K
items.explanation: Premature cessation of dual antiplatelet therapy early after a stent risks catastrophic stent thrombosis, so elective operations wait until the recommended duration is complete, and aspirin is generally continued through surgery. Stopping both now is unsafe. Platelet transfusion would not be needed and does not suit an elective case. Vitamin K does nothing to platelet inhibitors.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has persistent fever and candidemia from a central venous catheter after pancreatic surgery. He is hemodynamically stable and has not received prior azoles. Which management is correct?
options: Fluconazole alone while leaving the infected catheter in place for the whole course
Echinocandin therapy, catheter removal, and a dilated eye examination
Amphotericin only after discontinuing all antibiotics
Observation because candidemia is usually a contaminant of the blood culture bottle
items.explanation: Candida in a blood culture is never treated as a contaminant. An echinocandin is first-line for most patients, the line should be removed, and an ophthalmologic examination screens for endophthalmitis. Fluconazole is an option in stable azole-naive patients but leaving the catheter in place invites relapse. Stopping antibiotics does not help, and conventional amphotericin carries nephrotoxicity. Treatment continues two weeks beyond clearance.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man undergoes elective colectomy for cancer. The wound is classified as clean-contaminated. Which antibiotic regimen and timing best reduces the risk of surgical site infection?
options: Intravenous cefazolin with metronidazole given within 60 minutes before incision
Intravenous vancomycin alone given the night before the planned surgery date at the hospital
Oral neomycin only, started on the first day after the operation is finished
Intravenous ceftriaxone continued for five days after surgery
items.explanation: Colorectal prophylaxis needs activity against enteric gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, given within 60 minutes before incision, and usually with mechanical and oral antibiotic bowel preparation. Vancomycin alone lacks gram-negative coverage and is given too early. Postoperative-only oral dosing misses the incision window. Extended postoperative courses add resistance and toxicity without lowering infection rates. Prophylaxis ends within 24 hours.

items.stem: On postoperative day 8 after laparotomy for bowel obstruction, an obese 61-year-old woman has a gush of serosanguineous fluid from her midline incision. The skin is intact apart from the drainage, and she is afebrile. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Reassure and discharge with oral antibiotics
Cover with moist dressing, and take her to the operating room if evisceration is confirmed
Apply an adhesive skin closure over the drainage
Begin a high-protein diet and observe for a week
items.explanation: Sudden serosanguineous drainage around postoperative days 7 to 10 suggests fascial dehiscence, and an open wound should be checked for evisceration. Moist saline dressings and an abdominal binder protect the viscera while the patient is prepared for urgent re-closure if the fascia has separated. Discharge and antibiotics ignore the mechanical failure. Sealing the skin traps fluid and hides a defect. Observation risks evisceration.

items.stem: A patient has a transplanted organ that shows hyperacute rejection within minutes after reperfusion. Which pretransplant finding most likely explains this?
options: Preformed recipient antibodies against donor antigens
Donor lymphocytes attacking recipient tissues after transplantation of tissue
Late development of vascular intimal thickening over a period of years
Primary infection from a donor-derived virus acquired at the operation
items.explanation: Hyperacute rejection results from preformed antibodies, from ABO incompatibility or sensitization to HLA, that bind graft endothelium and activate complement, causing thrombosis and graft loss within minutes to hours. It is prevented by blood group matching and a negative crossmatch. Donor lymphocytes attacking host tissue describes graft-versus-host disease. Intimal thickening is chronic rejection. Viral infection presents later.

items.stem: Within minutes of a bee sting, a 38-year-old woman develops hives, wheezing, and hypotension. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction explains this presentation?
options: Type II, mediated by antibody against cell surface antigens and complement
Type III, mediated by circulating immune complexes
Type IV, mediated by sensitized T cells releasing cytokines over days
Type I, mediated by IgE bound to mast cells
items.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a type I hypersensitivity: preformed IgE on mast cells and basophils cross-links with antigen and releases histamine and other mediators within minutes. Type II involves antibody against cell antigens, as in hemolytic transfusion reactions. Type III results from immune complex deposition, as in serum sickness. Type IV is delayed, T cell driven, as in contact dermatitis. Intramuscular epinephrine is the first treatment.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man develops fever and a tender, fluctuant, erythematous 5-cm mass in the buttock with surrounding cellulitis. He is otherwise stable and has no systemic toxicity. Which treatment is most important?
options: Antibiotics alone for two weeks without any drainage procedure at all
Warm soaks and observation for a month
Incision and drainage, with antibiotics added only for selected features
Needle aspiration followed by repeated injections of antibiotic into the cavity
items.explanation: A fluctuant cutaneous abscess is treated by adequate incision and drainage, which is the primary therapy. Antibiotics are added when there is extensive cellulitis, systemic signs, immunosuppression, or a difficult location. Antibiotics alone fail because drugs poorly penetrate an abscess cavity. Soaks without drainage delay recovery. Needle aspiration has higher failure rates than incision, so it is not the standard approach.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has a high-risk bleeding profile after a major hip operation and needs thromboprophylaxis. She has severe renal impairment and a history of a drug-induced immune platelet disorder. Which agent is a suitable choice?
options: Fondaparinux, adjusted or avoided based on renal clearance and risk
A full-dose injectable anticoagulant from the class that caused the earlier event
Unfractionated anticoagulation given at a prophylactic dose twice daily
No prophylaxis because she has bleeding risk
items.explanation: Fondaparinux is a synthetic factor Xa inhibitor with minimal cross-reactivity in immune platelet disorders, so it is used after a prior event, but it is renally cleared and must be avoided or reduced when clearance is very low. Alternatives such as apixaban may be considered. The other injectable options belong to the drug classes that cause the disorder. Omitting prophylaxis ignores a high thrombosis risk.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has had five days of apixaban after a pulmonary embolism and now has a rectal bleed with hemodynamic instability. Which agent is the specific reversal option?
options: Protamine sulfate given by slow infusion
Andexanet alfa, or four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate if it is unavailable
Vitamin K given by mouth only, with a repeat level the next morning
Desmopressin given intravenously
items.explanation: Apixaban is a factor Xa inhibitor, and andexanet alfa is the specific agent that binds it. Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is a recognized alternative when andexanet is not available. Protamine neutralizes unfractionated anticoagulants and not oral factor Xa inhibitors. Vitamin K reverses warfarin slowly. Desmopressin helps platelet dysfunction and von Willebrand disease. Hemostatic measures and supportive resuscitation accompany reversal.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhea and a white count of 24,000 after a long course of ciprofloxacin. Stool testing confirms toxin-producing Clostridioides difficile. She has no ileus, hypotension, or megacolon. Which initial therapy is recommended?
options: Intravenous metronidazole as a single agent
Oral loperamide to slow gut motility and reduce stool frequency
Oral cefazolin with probiotic supplements added to the diet each day
Oral fidaxomicin, or oral vancomycin if fidaxomicin is unavailable
items.explanation: Current guidance favors oral fidaxomicin, with oral vancomycin as an acceptable alternative, for an initial episode. Metronidazole is now reserved for limited circumstances and intravenous metronidazole alone is not first-line. Antimotility agents risk toxic dilation. Cephalosporins would worsen the underlying dysbiosis. Fulminant disease with shock or ileus adds high-dose vancomycin, intravenous metronidazole, and colectomy consideration.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops a raised, firm, pink scar on the earlobe after piercing. Over a year the scar grows well beyond the original wound edges and extends into normal skin. Histology shows thick, haphazard collagen bundles. Which diagnosis fits best?
options: Hypertrophic scar, which stays confined to the wound borders
Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans of the earlobe
Keloid, extending past the original wound margins
Normal mature scar with expected remodeling
items.explanation: Keloids grow beyond the original wound, rarely regress, recur after simple excision, and show thick disorganized collagen. Hypertrophic scars stay within the wound edges and often improve over time. Dermatofibrosarcoma is a dermal sarcoma that does not follow a piercing in this way. A normal scar flattens and softens rather than expanding. Intralesional steroid, silicone, and combined excision with adjuvant therapy are used.

items.stem: A kidney transplant recipient is started on tacrolimus. Six weeks later she has tremor, hyperkalemia, and a rise in creatinine, with a high trough level. What is the principal mechanism of this drug?
options: Inhibition of purine synthesis in proliferating lymphocytes and other cells
Blockade of the interleukin-2 receptor on activated cells
Depletion of circulating lymphocytes by polyclonal antibody
Calcineurin inhibition, which blocks interleukin-2 transcription in T cells
items.explanation: Tacrolimus binds FK binding protein and inhibits calcineurin, preventing activation of the transcription factor that drives interleukin-2 gene expression. Its toxicities include nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, hyperkalemia, and new-onset diabetes, and trough levels guide dosing. Purine synthesis inhibition describes mycophenolate. Interleukin-2 receptor blockade describes basiliximab. Lymphocyte depletion describes antithymocyte globulin. Levels are monitored and doses adjusted for drug interactions.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has pneumonia and is admitted to the ward. Heart rate is 112, temperature 38.9 C, and a new confusion state is present. Blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg. Under current sepsis definitions, which finding best identifies sepsis rather than simple infection?
options: Acute organ dysfunction, such as an increase of two or more points in the organ failure score
Two or more systemic inflammatory response criteria alone, with no organ failure score being measured
A positive blood culture in any single bottle
A white blood cell count above twelve thousand
items.explanation: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, measured as an acute rise of two or more points in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score. Inflammatory criteria are nonspecific and appear in many noninfectious states. Blood cultures are positive in only a minority of septic patients. Leukocytosis alone reflects inflammation, not organ failure.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with a hemoglobin of 7.5 g per deciliter is stable and without cardiac disease after colectomy. Which transfusion threshold is supported by trial evidence?
options: Transfuse whenever hemoglobin is below 10 g per deciliter in any patient
Transfuse only after symptoms of shock appear
Transfuse when hemoglobin falls below 7 g per deciliter in most stable patients
Transfuse two units routinely before discharge in every postoperative patient on the ward
items.explanation: Randomized trials support a restrictive strategy with a threshold of 7 g per deciliter in hemodynamically stable patients, with a somewhat higher threshold for active coronary disease or ongoing ischemia. Liberal thresholds expose patients to more risk without better outcomes. Waiting for shock is unsafe. Routine transfusion before discharge has no basis, and each unit carries infectious, immune, and volume risks.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has fever, hypotension, and a distended tender abdomen four days after a bowel anastomosis. Imaging shows a pelvic fluid collection with extraluminal gas. She has received broad antibiotics for two days without improvement. What is the most important next intervention?
options: Escalation to a third antibiotic without any drainage procedure
Drainage of the collection to achieve source control
Continued observation with serial white counts
Initiation of total parenteral nutrition first
items.explanation: Persistent sepsis despite antibiotics in the presence of an undrained collection means the source has not been controlled, and drainage, percutaneous if accessible or operative if not, takes priority. Adding antibiotics cannot sterilize an abscess cavity. Observation delays treatment in an unstable patient. Nutrition support is secondary. Source control should occur as soon as is practical, ideally within hours of the diagnosis.

items.stem: A patient with prolonged sepsis has high circulating levels of a cytokine that causes fever through the hypothalamus and mediates cachexia. Which mediator is it?
options: Interleukin-4, the helper T cell type 2 cytokine
Interferon gamma only
Tumor necrosis factor alpha
Transforming growth factor beta
items.explanation: Tumor necrosis factor alpha and interleukin-1 are early pyrogenic mediators from activated macrophages. They cause fever, anorexia, and catabolism with muscle wasting, and in excess they promote septic shock. Interleukin-4 drives the helper T cell type 2 response and IgE class switching. Interferon gamma activates macrophages but is not the classic cachectic mediator. Transforming growth factor beta is mainly antiinflammatory and fibrotic.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has a plantar ulcer that has not progressed in eight weeks. Biopsy of the edge shows a prolonged inflammatory infiltrate with little granulation tissue. Which phase of healing is arrested in this chronic wound?
options: Remodeling phase, with excessive collagen cross-linking and scar maturation over months
Inflammatory phase, stalled before proliferation begins
Hemostasis phase, with failed platelet plug formation and clot
Maturation phase, with early scar contracture
items.explanation: Chronic wounds typically stall in a persistent inflammatory phase, driven by bacterial burden, ischemia, and hyperglycemia, so fibroblast proliferation and epithelialization never start. Remodeling occurs months later after a normal scar has formed. Hemostasis is complete within minutes and is not the problem here. Contracture belongs to late maturation. Treatment targets debridement, perfusion, glucose control, and offloading to restart the sequence.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with massive postpartum-type surgical bleeding is a Jehovah witness and has refused blood products in writing. She is competent and breathing. Which approach respects both her wishes and her care?
options: Honor her refusal and use bloodless measures, such as cell salvage in continuity, if she accepts
Transfuse over her objection because her life is at risk and time is short
Obtain a court order without discussing with her
Delay care until relatives agree to transfusion
items.explanation: A competent adult may refuse transfusion, and the surgeon honors the documented decision while offering every acceptable alternative, such as erythropoiesis support, meticulous hemostasis, tranexamic acid, and cell salvage only if she accepts a circuit in continuity with her circulation. Overriding her violates autonomy. Court orders apply to minors, not competent adults. Family cannot overrule her.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy has prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction, and his mother has heavy menses. Testing shows a prolonged bleeding time, a prolonged partial thromboplastin time, a normal platelet count, and low ristocetin cofactor activity. Which treatment is the first choice for minor bleeding?
options: Cryoprecipitate given weekly as prophylaxis for all family members
Platelet transfusion given before every procedure that involves a wound
Vitamin K given daily
Desmopressin, which releases stored von Willebrand factor
items.explanation: Von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder, causes mucosal bleeding with a prolonged partial thromboplastin time from low factor VIII. Desmopressin releases endothelial stores of von Willebrand factor and is first-line for most type 1 patients with minor bleeding. Cryoprecipitate is used for major bleeding when concentrate is unavailable. Platelets are normal. Vitamin K is for deficiency states.

items.stem: During a massive transfusion a 45-year-old woman develops hypotension, a prolonged QT interval, and tetany-like muscle twitching. Ionized calcium is low. What is the cause and treatment?
options: Citrate binding of calcium, treated with intravenous calcium
Hyperkalemia from stored red cells, treated with insulin and glucose alone
Transfusion-related lung injury, treated with diuretics
Hemolytic reaction, treated with alkalinization of urine
items.explanation: Stored blood contains citrate as an anticoagulant, which chelates ionized calcium, and the liver normally clears it. Rapid transfusion or liver failure causes hypocalcemia with hypotension, prolonged QT, and reduced myocardial function. Replace calcium intravenously and monitor ionized levels. Hyperkalemia would show peaked T waves. Lung injury causes hypoxemia. Hemolysis shows hemoglobinuria and fever, and treatment is supportive with calcium only when levels are low.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has a platelet count falling from 220,000 to 70,000 per microliter on day 7 of a hospital stay, with a new leg deep venous thrombosis. A drug-induced immune platelet disorder from an anticoagulant is suspected. Which management is correct?
options: Continue the same anticoagulant at a higher dose
Transfuse platelets promptly to raise the count
Switch to warfarin as the first step, while the platelet count is falling
Stop the offending anticoagulant and start argatroban, avoiding platelet transfusion
items.explanation: A platelet fall of more than half, five to ten days after exposure with new thrombosis, suggests immune-mediated platelet activation that is prothrombotic, not hemorrhagic. All exposure stops and a direct thrombin inhibitor such as argatroban is started. Increasing the same drug worsens thrombosis. Platelet transfusion may feed clotting. Warfarin alone risks venous limb gangrene and is delayed until counts recover.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man has a 12-cm chronic sacral pressure injury with healthy granulation tissue after sharp debridement and negative cultures. He is nonambulatory and has an albumin of 3.4. Which therapy best promotes wound contraction and reduces wound volume in this setting?
options: Daily wet-to-dry saline gauze dressing changes
Negative pressure wound therapy applied over a clean wound bed
Topical broad-spectrum antibiotic ointment applied to the wound twice daily
Immediate primary closure under tension
items.explanation: Negative pressure therapy applies subatmospheric pressure to a debrided bed, reducing edema, drawing edges together, and stimulating granulation and microdeformation. It should follow debridement and control of infection. Wet-to-dry dressings are nonselective and painful and do not match its performance. Topical antibiotics do not address mechanics. Closure under tension risks ischemia and dehiscence. Pressure offloading and nutrition remain prerequisites for success.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has a temperature rise to 38.8 C, rigors, and flank pain 10 minutes into a red cell transfusion. Urine is pink. Which immediate step is correct?
options: Slow the transfusion and give acetaminophen
Continue at the same rate and reassess the patient after the unit is done
Stop the transfusion, keep intravenous access, and send the unit and patient samples to the blood bank
Switch to a different unit from the same donor
items.explanation: Fever, rigors, flank pain, and hemoglobinuria soon after starting a transfusion suggest an acute hemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility, often from clerical error. The transfusion stops at once, access is kept for fluids, and the bag and samples are rechecked with the blood bank. Slowing or continuing risks fatal disseminated coagulation and renal failure. Using the same donor does not exclude error.
